title: Word order: verb, object, place and time
titleVi: Trật tự từ: động từ, tân ngữ, nơi chốn, thời gian
summary: Giữ động từ và tân ngữ sát nhau, xếp nơi chốn trước thời gian — trật tự câu tiếng Anh không linh hoạt như tiếng Việt.
whyItMatters: Tiếng Việt cho phép đảo trật tự khá tự do để nhấn mạnh; tiếng Anh thì không. *I very like this policy*, *He explained me the rule*, *She goes every day to work* đều hiểu được nhưng sai. Ở band 7.5, câu sai trật tự từ bị coi là lỗi **Grammatical Range and Accuracy** lặp lại, kéo điểm xuống dù từ vựng tốt.

sections.heading: The fixed spine: subject – verb – object
body: English word order is grammatical, not decorative. The basic spine is **subject → verb → object**: *The government introduced a new tax.* Change the order and you change the meaning or destroy the sentence.

Vietnamese often places the topic first and comments later, and it allows the object to move. English keeps the object after the verb: *The council rejected the plan*, never *The council the plan rejected*.
When you want to foreground information, do it with **time or place phrases at the front**, not by moving the object: *In 2019, the council rejected the plan.*

examples.right: The report identifies three causes of urban flooding.
examples.wrong: The report three causes of urban flooding identifies.

examples.right: In recent years, many graduates have left the capital.
examples.note: Time phrase fronted — normal and formal.

examples.right: The committee reviewed the evidence carefully.
examples.wrong: The committee reviewed carefully the evidence.
examples.note: Adverb does not split verb and object.

sections.heading: Place before time at the end of a sentence
body: When a sentence ends with both **place** and **time**, the neutral order is **place → time**: *She works **in a hospital** **six days a week**.* *They moved **to Da Nang** **in 2020**.*

Time can also move to the front for emphasis or to link with the previous sentence: *In 2020, they moved to Da Nang.* What it cannot do is sit between the verb and the place: *They moved in 2020 to Da Nang* is marked and unnatural in an essay.
With verbs of movement, the destination is part of the verb's core pattern, so it stays close: *arrive at the station*, *go to work*, *return to the office*.

examples.right: The family moved to the suburbs in 2018.
examples.wrong: The family moved in 2018 to the suburbs.

examples.right: Every morning, thousands of commuters crowd the metro.
examples.note: Time fronted — cohesive with the previous sentence.

examples.right: The clinic opens at seven in the morning.
examples.note: Fixed time expression stays after the verb.

sections.heading: Verb + object are a unit — do not insert adverbs
body: An adverb of manner or degree cannot sit between a verb and its object: *She speaks English fluently*, not *She speaks fluently English*. If the object is long, the adverb goes after it or before the verb.
The same rule explains why **very much** goes at the end: *I like this policy very much*, not *I like very much this policy*.

Some verbs take **object + preposition + person**, not two objects: *explain the rule **to** me*, *describe the process **to** us*, *suggest a solution **to** the committee*. *Explain me the rule* is a direct translation of *giải thích cho tôi*.

rows: suggest a plan to the board

sections.heading: Where adverbials go: manner, place, time
body: The full neutral order at the end of a clause is **manner → place → time**: *She sang beautifully at the concert last night.* This is the same order you need in Task 1 descriptions: *The figure rose sharply in 2010.*
Short frequency adverbs go in **mid position**, before the main verb or after *be*: *The city **always** invests in transport*, *The city is **always** short of funds.*

Long prepositional phrases prefer the end. Putting a long phrase mid-sentence forces the reader to hold the verb in memory: *The council, after months of consultation with residents and experts, approved the plan* is acceptable because it is set off by commas; without commas it becomes unreadable.

examples.right: The figure rose sharply in the final quarter.
She has always worked in the public sector.
examples.note: Frequency adverb after the first auxiliary.

examples.right: The council approved the plan after months of consultation.
examples.note: Long phrase at the end, where it is easy to process.

sections.heading: Fronting: when it helps, when it hurts
body: Fronting a **time** or **place** phrase is standard academic practice because it creates a smooth link with the previous sentence: *In rural areas, access to specialist care remains limited.*

Fronting an **object** is much more restricted. It appears in speech and journalism for contrast — *This problem the government has ignored for years* — but in an essay it reads as inversion without a trigger. Use a cleft instead: *It is this problem that the government has ignored for years.*

Negative fronting requires **inversion** and belongs to C1 style: *Never has the city faced such pressure.* If you front a negative adverbial without inverting the subject and verb, the sentence is wrong.

examples.right: In coastal provinces, fishing communities face the greatest risk.
examples.note: Fronted place phrase — cohesive and formal.

examples.right: It is this problem that the government has ignored for years.
examples.note: Cleft keeps the emphasis without breaking order.

examples.right: Never has the city faced such pressure on housing.
examples.wrong: Never the city has faced such pressure on housing.
examples.note: Negative fronting forces inversion: *has the city*.

commonMistakes.right: I really like this policy. / I like this policy very much.
commonMistakes.why: **very** không đứng trước động từ thường. Dùng *really* trước động từ, hoặc *very much* ở cuối câu.

commonMistakes.wrong: The teacher explained me the rule.
commonMistakes.right: The teacher explained the rule to me.
commonMistakes.why: **explain** không nhận hai tân ngữ. Cấu trúc là `explain something to somebody`, dịch sát *giải thích cái gì cho ai*.

commonMistakes.wrong: She goes every day to the office.
commonMistakes.right: She goes to the office every day.
commonMistakes.why: Trật tự cuối câu là **nơi chốn → thời gian**. Đặt thời gian trước nơi chốn nghe rất *Việt*.

commonMistakes.wrong: The committee reviewed carefully the proposal.
commonMistakes.right: The committee reviewed the proposal carefully.
commonMistakes.why: Trạng từ không chen giữa động từ và tân ngữ. Tân ngữ phải đứng ngay sau động từ.

commonMistakes.wrong: Never the city has faced such pressure.
commonMistakes.right: Never has the city faced such pressure.
commonMistakes.why: Khi đưa trạng từ phủ định lên đầu câu, phải **đảo ngữ**: trợ động từ đứng trước chủ ngữ.

ieltsTips: Dùng cụm **thời gian/nơi chốn** ở đầu câu để tạo mạch liên kết giữa các câu trong đoạn Task 2: *In rural districts, the shortage is even more acute.* Câu sau nối trực tiếp với ý trước mà không cần *however* hay *moreover*.
Trong Task 1, giữ đúng thứ tự **manner → place → time** khi mô tả số liệu: *Unemployment fell sharply in the north in 2019.* Nếu đảo, câu vẫn hiểu được nhưng mất tự nhiên.
Tuyệt đối không chen trạng từ giữa động từ và tân ngữ. Nếu câu dài, đưa trạng từ ra cuối: *The government introduced the new tax on single-use plastics without warning.*
Hạn chế đảo tân ngữ lên đầu trong Writing. Muốn nhấn mạnh, dùng **câu chẻ** (*It is this issue that…*) hoặc **đảo ngữ với trạng từ phủ định** (*Never has…*) — cả hai đều đúng chuẩn học thuật.

exercises.question: Which sentence has correct word order?
options: The council rejected carefully the plan.
The council very rejected the plan.
exercises.explanation: Subject → verb → object, with no adverb between verb and object.

exercises.question: They moved ___ .
exercises.explanation: Place before time: **to the suburbs in 2018**.

exercises.question: She speaks ___ .
exercises.explanation: Verb and object stay together; the adverb follows the object.

exercises.question: Could you ___ ?
exercises.explanation: **explain something to somebody** — no double object.

exercises.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: Never the city has faced such pressure.
Never has the city faced such pressure.
Never the city faced has such pressure.
The city never has faced such pressure.
exercises.explanation: Negative fronting requires inversion: **Never has the city faced…**

exercises.question: I like this policy very ___ .
exercises.explanation: **very much** goes at the end, after the object.

exercises.question: The teacher explained the rule ___ me.
She goes to the office ___ (every / day).
exercises.explanation: Place (*to the office*) before time (*every day*).

exercises.question: The figure rose ___ (sharp) in the final quarter.
___ rural areas, access to specialist care remains limited.
exercises.explanation: **In rural areas** — a fronted place phrase needs the preposition.
